Ellipse Focal

CurvesGeometryCoordinates
Game: This shows an ellipse and its two foci, with a number that stays the same wherever you move on the curve.
How to play: Drag the four corners of the dashed box to reshape the ellipse, or drag the point P. You can also focus a dot and use the arrow keys; press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

An ellipse can be drawn with two pins and a loop of string. The page for this applet says the curve is the set of points whose distances from the two pins add to the same number. The picture here lets you check that sentence yourself.

The page's claim, checked

The exact claim is PF + PF' = const: move the point P anywhere on the curve and the two distances to the foci still add up to one fixed length. The logic test checked 11,664 points on 324 differently shaped ellipses; the largest change in that sum was less than one ten-millionth of a unit. So the page's claim holds here, and the constant is twice the longer half of the dashed box.

This is a different test from the one on the neighbouring page Focus and Directrix of Ellipse. That page uses one focus and a line, and says the ratio of the two distances is a fixed number below 1: dist(P,F) / dist(P,d) = const < 1. That number is the eccentricity. This applet draws no directrix and compares no ratio; it only adds two focal distances. Both descriptions pick out the same conic, but they are not the same statement.

Where the foci sit

Let the dashed box have half-widths A and B, measured from its middle. The longer one is the semi-major axis a and the shorter is b. Each focus is c = sqrt(a² − b²) from the middle, along the long direction: side to side if the box is wider, up and down if it is taller. The test checks both directions, including boxes turned the other way round. When the box is a square, c = 0: the two foci merge at the centre and the ellipse is a circle, with sum 2a.

Why the little bar matches the curve

The applet measures d1 = PF and d2 = PF', then lays a two-piece bar below (or beside) the picture. Its first piece has length d1, its second has length d2. That is why the red ray and the first bar piece match, and the blue ray and the second match: the whole bar is d1 + d2, the same fixed sum, whatever P does. The bar sits along the top when the rectangle is wider than it is tall and down the left edge otherwise, as in the original.

What changed from the Java applet

The Java canvas is now an SVG with focusable, arrow-key-movable dots; the green panel and grey buttons are gone, and a Reset button has been added (the original had no buttons). Small F, F′ and P labels are shown, though the applet's unused ShowNames flag left them out. Two quirks stay: a corner drag into the small middle square is refused, and P is snapped by feeding its scaled offsets to a signed-angle helper whose reference point sits 200 units to the right of the centre, so a drag can land somewhere other than the nearest point of the curve. The logic test compares that step with a second transcription of the bytecode rather than silently fixing it. There is no win or loss: the original page calls this an illustration.

Try making the dashed box a square: the two foci meet in the middle and the bar becomes two copies of the radius. Then stretch it sideways and watch the foci travel onto the long axis.
